newsitem.title: GERMANY: German defence minister confident of NATO deal.
newsitem.headline: German defence minister confident of NATO deal.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Tuesday that he was confident Russia would sign an agreement paving the way for NATO's planned expansion soon even if negotiations proved difficult.

Speaking at a conference on security issues in the southern German village of Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Ruehe said the negotiations between NATO and Russia had entered a decisive phase ahead of a NATO summit in Madrid in July.

"It is no secret that the negotiations with Russia have entered into a decisive phase," Ruehe said, according to a text of his speech. "Even if the negotiations are difficult, I am confident that the agreement will soon be signed by government and state leaders."

Russian President Boris Yeltsin, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais have seized opportunities in recent days to criticise NATO's plans to offer membership to countries once in the Soviet bloc.

Yeltsin signalled at a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki last month that he had accepted the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's expansion was inevitable, although he still regards it as a security threat.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are front-runners to join the Western alliance.
"Before the (Madrid) summit there will most probably be a binding agreement at the highest level with Russia for an extensive security partnership," Ruehe said.
The German minister said there were larger issues at stake in the talks that the public was missing.
"It's not about expansion or a good relationship to Russia," Ruehe said. "It is not about damage control or ostracising or isolating. That is the language of the old way of thinking.
"The key term of our policies is stability," Ruehe said.
He said it would be "immoral" to exclude countries such as Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary from NATO.

"We do not have military enemies any more," Ruehe said. "But there is a series of new, complex risks. The enemy today is instability...It is our duty to establish stability in Europe itself, but also in the bordering regions."
